extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of psychoanalysis, literary critics, and researchers of humor theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the formal techniques that produce jokes (linguistic and psychical mechanisms), identifying processes such as condensation, modification, multiple use of verbal material, double meaning, and related subtypes with examples and diagnostic notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation (formation of substitutes / composite words)
rubrics_metrics.description: A psychical/linguistic process in which two ideas or elements are fused, producing abbreviation and substitute-formations (e.g., composite words); condensation is responsible for the verbal expression of many jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud describes condensation as creating composite structures or interpenetration of constituents (example: the fusion of ‘boring’ and ‘Faden’ into a condensed insulting phrase). Condensation both shortens wording and creates a substitute whose verbal form is essential to the joke’s effect. Example: ‘roter Faden’ fused into a jibe about a red-haired person. Note: condensation often underlies the brevity and substitute-formation of effective jokes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Condensation accompanied by slight modification
rubrics_metrics.description: A variant of condensation where one component is slightly altered (a letter or sound change, small addition) so that the omitted or suppressed insult/thought is nevertheless indicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include turning a t into a b in ‘tête-à-tête’ → ‘tête-à-bête’ to imply ‘ass’, and replacing ‘before’ with ‘behind’ in ‘great future behind him’. Freud notes that the slighter the modification the better the joke technically. This technique produces substitutes without forming a striking composite word.

rubrics_metrics.name: Brevity of a particular kind (resulting from substitute-formation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes often display 'brevity' that is specifically the product of condensation/substitute-formation rather than mere laconic speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jean Paul’s aphorism 'the soul of wit' is quoted but Freud emphasizes brevity alone does not constitute a joke; the brevity must leave behind a trace (a substitute-formation) produced by the condensation process. Thus shortness plus evidence of a condensed substitute is a criterion of joke technique.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple use of the same verbal material (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: The technique of using identical or closely related words/phrases multiple times in a sentence, with differing senses or slight alterations, to produce comic effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This umbrella category includes several subtypes (syllable-splitting, rearrangement, slight modification, double meaning). Freud treats previously-known 'play' as a technical family he terms 'multiple use'. Example varieties span from whole-word reuse to modified repeats.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of a name once whole and again divided into syllables (syllable-splitting / charade technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: A name is used in two ways in the same utterance: once intact and again parsed into syllables that convey a different sense (e.g., 'Rousseau' → 'roux et sot').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: the 'roux et sot' quip on Rousseau, Antigone → ‘Antik? Oh, nee.’ This species depends on the double exploitation of the name’s sound/segments. Freud notes this as a distinct method of multiple use, producing jokes without condensation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrangement/rearrangement of identical material (inversion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Keeping the same verbal material but altering its arrangement or order so that what is said in the same words appears different and comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: 'Some think husband has earned a lot and so has been able to lay by a bit; others think wife has lain back a bit and so has been able to earn a lot.' The slighter the alteration of arrangement, the stronger the technical effect. Economy of means and minimal alteration increase comic power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Slight orthographic/phonetic modification (single-letter/near-homophone changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Changing a letter or sound minimally so that two similar forms contrast (or imply an omitted thought) and create humor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ‘antesemitism’ vs ‘anti-semitism’; single-letter changes that easily go unnoticed in careless speech. This overlaps with condensation-with-modification but can operate without condensation, relying on near-homophony or tiny orthographic shifts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words / double meaning (general)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of a word that legitimately carries two meanings in context so that both meanings are activated simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud subdivides this into (a) double meaning of a name and its referent, (b) literal vs metaphorical meanings, and (c) pure double meaning where the word as-is expresses two senses. Examples: Napoleon’s 'vol' (flight/theft), 'The King is not a subject.' The pure double-meaning case is an 'ideal' form of multiple use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double meaning of a name and of the thing named (name-play)
rubrics_metrics.description: A name and the thing/meaning it denotes are used to exploit two senses (punning on proper nouns or place names).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'Discharge thyself of our company, Pistol!' and local-toponym jokes (Hof/Freiung in Vienna), 'On Elsa’s account' (Elsa/Elsass). Can involve slight modification where unaltered use is impossible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literal versus metaphorical double meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: A word is used so that both its literal, concrete sense and its metaphorical/figurative sense are activated to produce a comic link.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the laryngoscope/mirror pun about Dr. Schnitzler’s son holding up a mirror to contemporaries (literal instrument vs metaphoric actor). This source is highly fertile for jokes that hinge on conceptual juxtaposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Play upon words proper (pure double meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: The word as it stands expresses two different meanings without modification or cutting—an ideal case of multiple use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: French quips about 'vol' (flight/theft), the courtier: 'Le roi n'est pas sujet.' Freud regards these as particularly clear instances of the technique; they require favorable circumstances in context to activate both meanings at once.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double entendre (sexual double meaning)
rubrics_metrics.description: Subgroup of double meaning where one sense is sexual/erotic and the other is non-sexual; the sexual sense is often covert or less obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'innocence' (legal/sexual) in the Dreyfus joke, Spitzer’s 'laid back/lay by' example where the sexual meaning may be hidden. Freud notes that in some jokes the sexual meaning is prominent, in others it is covered and might escape notice—this concealment can be crucial to the joke’s effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unification (defining by means of itself)
rubrics_metrics.description: A technique in which a concept is defined or unified through repetition or by using its own term to create an intimate linkage (self-referential definition).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Schleiermacher’s 'Eifersucht is a Leidenschaft which mit Eifer sucht what Leiden schafft' and the 'ordentlich/ausserordentlich' joke. Produces an ingenious interlacement or 'unification' that contributes to comic effect even in the absence of other features.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ready repartee / reparative reuse of words (quick retort technique)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the same words or nearly the same phrasing uttered by another to produce an immediate comic retort or punishment (often at the expense of the interlocutor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: the jurisprudence exam 'Labeo ait' → 'I fall, says he.' 'You fail, say I.' Freud links this technique to multiple use; it functions as a quick, context-sensitive use of the verbal material for comedic reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound-joke (Klangwitz) / phonetic identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes relying principally on identity or near-identity of sounds rather than omission or condensation (e.g., puns based on homophones or dialect pronunciation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rousseau/roux et sot is classified as a 'Klangwitz' where no omission or condensation occurs; the joke rests on sound identity alone. Also example: Berlin dialect Antigone → 'Antik? Oh, nee.' Freud notes these are sometimes of an 'inferior sort' but can be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full vs watered-down (full/empty) morphological identity
rubrics_metrics.description: Where a full word and a reduced or suffixal form derived from the same stem have identical pronunciation, allowing simultaneous activation of a full meaning and a diminished (watered-down) meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Lichtenberg’s blind/lame exchange 'How are you getting along?' — 'As you see.' In German, identity between a full word and a suffix allows jokes where one reading is 'full' and the other 'empty', and the joke exploits the switch between them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sense-and-nonsense diagnostic (words simultaneously sense and nonsense)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deliberate use of phrasing that, given prior context, will be read both as a coherent sense and as nonsense, producing comic bewilderment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Freud’s Saphir/Rothschild example: reuse of creditor’s words so that they can be read as 'You come about the money' or 'You are losing the money', making the reply both sense and nonsense. Freud explains how this produces a comic situation by simultaneous activation of incompatible interpretations.
